### eDNA Datasets:

The data I will use today are a couple of eDNA datasets I have laying around. They are optimization tests, so in other words, I used these data a long time ago to make decisions about what methods to use moving forward.

However, I never properly looked at them myself! I want to change that.

First, load in the data:

```{r}

# this one is a comparison of different taq polymerases
taq_test <- readr::read_csv(here("Week_08", "Data", "zotu_table.csv"))

# this one is a comparison between different primer multiplexes
mf_mplex_test <- readr::read_csv(here("Week_08", "Data", "fish_mp_data.csv"))


```

These two datasets are similar in structure, but were processed at different times and so have slight differences. The taq_test document is older, and so "NA" is used when taxonomy was uncertain. The mf_mplex_test was run after updates to our bioinformatics pipeline, replacing this with the word "dropped".

What I plan to do with these datasets is as follows: 

 1. Make a simple function that will clean up the data by subtracting the contents of the negative controls (user specified) from all other samples, and then zeroes out any negatives. Make it flexible across both datasets.
 
 2. Make a plotting function that allows for quick comparison across samples.
 
 
### eDNA Data Cleaning Function:
 
See below for the details regarding the data cleaning function - clean_eDNA()

```{r}


# set up the function with the following variables:
#    data = your dataframe
#    first_sample_ID = the first sample column name when reading from left to right
#    control_IDs = any negative or positive control column names, as they vary from file to file and thus should be specified in this case. If my data entry organization was better in the past, I wouldn't have to have this!

clean_eDNA <- function(data, first_sample_ID, control_IDs) {
  
  data |> 
    #remove everything that does not have a domain
    filter(domain != "" | domain != "dropped") -> noblank_data
    
  noblank_data |> 
    #pull the names of the sample columns
    select({{first_sample_ID}}:last_col()) |> 
    colnames() -> sample_cols
  
  # Add a new row called neg_totals that is the sum of every negative column specified
  noblank_data |> 
    mutate(neg_totals = rowSums(noblank_data[, {{control_IDs}}], na.rm = TRUE)) |> 

  # Edit all sample columns to subtract this new negative sum column
    mutate(across(all_of(sample_cols), ~ .x - neg_totals)) |> 

  # change all negative numbers across all of the sample columns to zeros
    mutate(across(all_of(sample_cols), ~ ifelse(.x < 0, 0, .x))) |> 
  
  # remove the neg_totals row
    select(1:(last_col()-1)) -> clean_need_sum
  
  # add sum column of all sample columns
  clean_need_sum |> 
    mutate(sample_sums = rowSums(clean_need_sum[, sample_cols], na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  
  # remove any rows that have a zero sum after subtracting negative controls
    filter(sample_sums != 0) |> 
    
  # remove the sample_sums row
    select(1:(last_col()-1)) |> 
  
  # remove all negative control columns 
    select(-all_of({{control_IDs}})) -> cleaned_eDNA
  
  return(cleaned_eDNA)
}

  
```
 

Alright, letʻs see how it works with the datasets:

```{r}

# This is the dataset I used to build the function:

clean_eDNA(data = taq_test, 
           first_sample_ID = "T10_S31_L001", 
           control_IDs = c("T10_S31_L001", "T15_S36_L001", 
                           "T20_S41_L001", "T25_S46_L001", 
                           "T30_S51_L001", "T35_S56_L001", 
                           "T40_S61_L001", "T5_S26_L001")) -> clean_taq_test

#it works! Let's try it with the other dataset:

clean_eDNA(data = mf_mplex_test,
           first_sample_ID = "EQ_MFE_1",
           control_IDs = c("EQ_MFE_Neg", "EQ_MFU_Neg", "EQ_MF_E_U_Neg", 
                           "Q5_MFE_Neg", "Q5_MFU_Neg", "Q5_MF_E_U_Neg")) -> clean_mfu_test

#Nice! It worked!
```

### Plotting Function

For this section, I will be making a function that pivots long and plots the eDNA data cleaned from the previous function for quick visualization. I would like to make it compatible with both the clean and pre-cleaned data, for easy comparisons.


```{r}

# create function
plot_eDNA <- function(data, first_sample_ID, plotby_taxa = phylum, stack_or_fill = "stack",
                      domains = "none", kingdoms = "none", phyla = "none", classes = "none",
                      orders = "none", families = "none", genera = "none", specieses = "none") {
  
  # set up labels for later based on argument inputs
  if (stack_or_fill == "stack") {
    y_axis <- "Number of Sequences"
    title_text <- "eDNA Sequence Summary Plot"
  } else if (stack_or_fill == "fill") {
    y_axis <- "Relative Amount of Sequences"
    title_text <- "eDNA Relative Sequence Summary Plot"
  }
  
  ################ Filter by identities:
  
# if domain is specified, filter the data by the domains specified
  if (length(domains) == 1 && domains == "none") {
    data <- data
  } else {
    data <- filter(data, domain %in% domains)
  }
  
  # if kindom is specified, filter the data by the kingdoms specified
  if (length(kingdoms) == 1 && kingdoms == "none") {
    data <- data
  } else {
    data <- filter(data, kingdom %in% kingdoms)
  }
  
  # if phylum is specified, filter the data by the phyla specified
  if (length(phyla) == 1 && phyla == "none") {
    data <- data
  } else {
    data <- filter(data, phylum %in% phyla)
  }
  
  # if class is specified, filter the data by the classes specified
  if (length(classes) == 1 && classes == "none") {
    data <- data
  } else {
    data <- filter(data, class %in% classes)
  }
  
  # if order is specified, filter the data by the orders specified
  if (length(orders) == 1 && orders == "none") {
    data <- data
  } else {
    data <- filter(data, order %in% orders)
  }
  
  # if family is specified, filter the data by the families specified
  if (length(families) == 1 && families == "none") {
    data <- data
  } else {
    data <- filter(data, family %in% families)
  }
  
  # if genus is specified, filter the data by the genera specified
  if (length(genera) == 1 && genera == "none") {
    data <- data
  } else {
    data <- filter(data, genus %in% genera)
  }
  
  # if species is specified, filter the data by the species specified 
  # hilariously, I had to make this argument "specieses" as I can't have it be "species" D:
  if (length(specieses) == 1 && specieses == "none") {
    data <- data
  } else {
    data <- filter(data, species %in% specieses)
  }
  
  # call data
  data |> 
    
    # retrieve the sample column names again
    select({{first_sample_ID}}:last_col()) |> 
    colnames() -> sample_cols
  
  # call it again
  data |> 
    
    #pivot the data longer to better plot with
    pivot_longer(cols = sample_cols,
                 names_to = "site",
                 values_to = "num_sequences") -> long_eDNA
  
  # and plot!
  long_eDNA |> 
    ggplot(mapping = aes(x = site,
                         y = num_sequences,         # base plot, fill by specified taxa
                         fill = {{plotby_taxa}})) +
    geom_col(position = stack_or_fill) +
    theme_dark() +
    coord_flip() +                               #theming and aethetics
    scale_fill_viridis_d() +
    theme(title = element_text(face = "bold",
                               size = 25),
          axis.title = element_text(size = 15)) +
    labs(title = title_text,
         subtitle = "Use arguments to refine if needed",
         caption = "Note: Any gap between 0 sequences and the column's beginning are unidentified sequences.",
         x = "Site / Sample Name",               # labels
         y = y_axis) -> eDNA_plot
    
  return(eDNA_plot)
  
}

```

Finally, it is extremely difficult to see color differences between taxa in many of these charts because there are too many at once. I have made it so that we can isolate specific orders, families, genera, etc. with the following arguments: (default = "none", but these can be changed out for concatenated names to select specific groups at once.)

 - domains = "none"
 
 - kingdoms = "none"
 
 - phyla = "none"
 
 - classes = "none"
 
 - orders = "none" 

 - families = "none" 
 
 - genera = "none"
 
 - specieses = "none" 
  
   - (Note: yes, this pains me as well as it is not the plural of "species", but it must be disctinct from the column named "species" in the dataset.)

I have now added extra arguments to the function above that filter by categories specified.

For example below, I have filtered the cleaned Taq test data by domain Eukaryota only:

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| label: fig-eDNA5
#| fig-cap: "eDNA Summary for the Taq test dataset by Phyla, with only lines from domain Eukaryota. Note that every single sample is from the same exact site, so similarities in composition across these samples are expected."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7



plot_eDNA(clean_taq_test, T11_S32_L001, domains = "Eukaryota")


#ggsave(here("Week_08", "Output", "eDNAplot5.png"),
#       width = 11,
#       height = 7)

```

Below I have selected only orders Zoantharia, Haplosclerida, and Nudibranchia, then plotted by family:

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| label: fig-eDNA6
#| fig-cap: "eDNA Summary for the Taq test dataset by family, with only lines from the orders Zoantharia, Haplosclerida, and Nudibranchia. Note that every single sample is from the same exact site, so similarities in composition across these samples are expected."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7


# order filter test
plot_eDNA(clean_taq_test, T11_S32_L001, plotby_taxa = family, orders = c("Zoantharia", "Haplosclerida", "Nudibranchia"))

#ggsave(here("Week_08", "Output", "eDNAplot6.png"),
#       width = 11,
#       height = 7)

```

These arguments can be stacked, but note that the spelling must be exact.
